extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; economists and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and exposition of the laws that determine how the produce of a community is divided among land (rent), labor (wages), and capital (interest), with critique of existing political-economy formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages as direct produce of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Each productive laborer, as he works, creates his wages; wages do not come from capital but are the direct produce of labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text insists that 'each productive laborer produces his own wages' and that with every additional laborer there is an addition to the true wages fund—an addition to the common stock of wealth, generally greater than the amount he draws in wages. This rejects theories that treat wages as paid out of a pre-existing capital fund.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population density increases productive power
rubrics_metrics.description: The denser the population the more minute becomes the subdivision of labor, the greater the economies of production and distribution, and a greater number of people can produce a larger proportionate amount of wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by comparing older, populous countries (e.g., England, Massachusetts) with new countries (e.g., California early years, New Zealand), arguing that increasing population typically increases per-capita production because of improved infrastructure, specialization, and economies of scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulated wealth is ephemeral and limited in effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth can be accumulated only to a slight degree; many forms decay and require constant labor to preserve and renew; present consumption cannot be explained chiefly by past accumulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cities rebuilt after fires (London 1666, Chicago 1870) quickly regain wealth under labor; accumulated wealth plays only a modest, temporary role (like stored nutriment), so differences in consumption chiefly reflect current production, not past hoards.

rubrics_metrics.name: The problem of poverty lies in distribution, not production
rubrics_metrics.description: The enigma of poverty amid advancing wealth arises not from insufficient productive power but from mal-adjustments in the laws of distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because production per capita often rises while the lowest classes remain poor, the text narrows inquiry to the laws which determine what part of the produce goes to labor (wages), capital (interest), and landowners (rent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution must be analyzed as division among land, labor, and capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The produce of a community is distributed among three factors—land (natural opportunities), labor (human exertion), and capital (wealth used to produce more wealth)—and the corresponding shares are rent, wages, and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking the laws of distribution one must keep these three returns separate; the produce means wealth above what is necessary to replace consumed capital; taxation and monopoly can be treated as reducing the produce but need not alter the fundamental division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminological precision: use 'interest' for return to capital, separate from 'profits'
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits (common usage) aggregate wages of superintendence, compensation for risk, and interest; for distributional analysis the correct exclusive term for the return to capital is 'interest'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes standard works that confuse profits and interest and advises consistently using 'interest' to signify that part of the produce which goes to capital, reserving 'wages' for rewards of human exertion and 'rent' for returns to natural opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of distribution must be correlated and proportional
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of distribution are laws of proportion and must be so related that any two being given the third may be inferred; the parts of a whole are mutually determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies: if Tom, Dick, and Harry are partners, fixing two shares fixes the third. The current disparate statements of wages, rent, and interest in political economy lack this necessary mutual relation, indicating errors in at least two of the three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of wages-fund theory (wages determined by capital-to-labor ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: The common doctrine that wages are determined by the ratio between the amount of capital devoted to payment/subsistence of labor and the number of laborers is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that this preaccepted theory cannot explain observed facts (e.g., wages highest where they are lowest in reality) and has led economists to contract 'wages' to a narrow sense, contributing to terminological confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural order: land, then labor, then capital (capital is result of labor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital is not the prime factor that employs labor; the natural genesis is land → labor → capital: land enables labor, labor creates capital (stored-up labor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because labor can produce without capital (and capital is produced by labor), laws of rent and wages must correlate without reference to capital; capital's law must be subordinate so the distribution laws work even when capital's role is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic definition of rent (exclusive right to natural opportunities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rent is the share in the wealth produced which the exclusive right to the use of natural capabilities gives to the owner; it excludes payments for the use of human-made improvements (these are interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes common speech (rent of houses includes improvements) from economic meaning: only that part paid for the use of land (natural opportunities) is rent. Payments for buildings/machinery are returns to capital (interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rent exists even when owner and user are same; rent can be actual or potential
rubrics_metrics.description: In the economic sense rent occurs where the same person is owner and user—what he could obtain by letting is rent; land value and rent can be capitalized in sale price; land unused but with value has potential rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wherever land has exchange value there is rent; its capacity to yield rent gives land value. The presence of rent does not depend on separate owner/user relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rent arises from relative scarcity compared to other land (margin of cultivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rent does not arise from the productiveness or utility of land per se but from its capacity as compared with land that can be had for nothing—the difference above what equal application of labor and capital could procure from the poorest land in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very rich plot yields no rent if equally good land is freely available; when superior land is scarce (i.e., better than the best free land), it begins to have value and yield rent. This restates the law of rent determined by the margin of cultivation.
